title: Hera Systems POC scoping - Latency SLOs & Benchmarks
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, and a measurement plan for the Hera Systems pilot. Agreed on p95/p99 targets for both TTFT and TPOT for interactive and batch workloads. Redwood to provide benchmark harness, baseline results, and security docs; Hera to share sample traffic profiles and deployment constraints. Next steps: share scripts, schedule pilot kickoff, run baseline tests next week.

p95/p99 SLO targets for interactive chat & batch inference
Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, batch sizes
Environment: hosted vs dedicated vs private, network egress

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-18 14:00 UTC | Duration 48m | Attendees: Ivy (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Sanjay (Hera ML), Evelyn (Hera Platform), Laura (Hera PM)

Summary (auto): Quick intro, align on success criteria for POC (latency & throughput SLOs), define measurement plan and deliverables.

00:00 - Ivy Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro on our side — Ivy, AE, Marco SE.
00:18 - Sanjay Rao: yep thanks, Sanjay here, we'll be leading the ML side. We want to validate production latency under our typical load and see cost tradeoffs.
00:35 - Marco Diaz: great, today we want to walk TTFT vs TPOT, get your target p95/p99 for interactive vs batch, and nail down the measurement plan.
01:02 - Evelyn Park: quick note — our infra team prefers private or dedicated; data residency and KMS are big for us. We'll share the security checklist later.
01:30 - Ivy Chen: noted. On SLOs: we usually separate TTFT (time to first token) for chat/interactive and TPOT (time per output token) for streaming scenarios; does that match your definitions?
02:05 - Laura Kim: yes, for our product interactive chat is judged on TTFT, but generative long-running jobs care about TPOT and overall throughput. Slight stutter there was — ok.
02:40 - Sanjay Rao: what do you recommend for p95/p99 targets? We currently aim for p95 < 400ms for TTFT and p99 < 700ms, but that's on our internal infra.
03:05 - Marco Diaz: realistic starting points: for hosted low-latency models, p95 TTFT 200-400ms, p99 600-900ms depending on model size and sequence length. For TPOT p95 ~20-40ms per token and p99 ~60-120ms per token. But this varies with batching and KV cache.
03:42 - Sanjay Rao: hmm ok. Our median token length is ~12 tokens per request, but we have a long tail up to 512. Token histogram will help.
04:10 - Ivy Chen: yes please share token histogram. For SLOs it's important to pick target sequence lengths: short (<=32), medium (33-128), long (>128). We'll run separate bench buckets.
04:45 - Evelyn Park: also we care about tail-latency on p99 because our UX surfaces slow responses to customers. So p99 is critical.
05:05 - Marco Diaz: agree — our measurement plan will collect both first-token hist and per-token latency distributions, plus concurrency/queueing metrics. We'll report p50/p95/p99 and 99.9 if needed.
05:40 - Laura Kim: what about TPOT vs aggregated throughput? We expect bursty QPS around 120 QPS with spikes to 350 for short windows. Sustained baseline is 60 QPS.
06:10 - Marco Diaz: good data; we'll size the pilot to replicate that: sustained 60 qps, concurrency target 40, peak bursts to 350 qps for 2-5 minutes. We'll test both single-user TTFT and sustained TPOT.
06:45 - Sanjay Rao: do you recommend dedicated for this or hosted with reserved capacity? Our priority is predictability and compliant data handling.
07:05 - Ivy Chen: for predictability and data isolation, Dedicated is common — predictable throughput and SLA. Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) is optional if you need strict network controls and on-prem KMS. Hosted can work but you'd rely on Redwood's tenancy and egress controls.
07:45 - Evelyn Park: can you run benchmarks in our VPC? Or do you need a sample payload?
08:02 - Marco Diaz: we can run the benchmark runner from a controlled environment; for VPC we'd ask for a small test subnet and an SSH jump or we run a client in your cloud account. Otherwise, we run a synthetic workload from Redwood and you validate results.
08:30 - Sanjay Rao: security — SOC2 and ISO docs? any attestation for data at rest and KMS?
08:50 - Ivy Chen: yes we'll send SOC2 and ISO summaries, KMS integrations (customer-managed keys) are supported for Dedicated and Private. We'll attach the security pack after this call.
09:10 - Laura Kim: back to measurement: how do you measure TTFT when streaming vs non-streaming models — difference in instrumentation?
09:30 - Marco Diaz: we instrument at the API gateway and model runtime. TTFT is measured from request arrival to the moment first token is emitted at the client-facing stream. For non-streaming we measure server-to-client first byte. For TPOT we measure token emission intervals and aggregate per-token latencies. We also capture queue time, batching delay, and GPU compute time.
10:05 - Sanjay Rao: do you account for network jitter? We want client-side SLOs too; network can add 50-100ms.
10:25 - Marco Diaz: yes we'll separate network+client RTT vs server processing. We'll provide both server-side and end-to-end metrics; for end-to-end you can run a remote agent in your VPC.
10:50 - Ivy Chen: let's define success criteria for the POC: 1) reproduce baseline latency under your token distribution and qps, 2) meet agreed p95/p99 targets for TTFT and TPOT in short/medium/long buckets, 3) demonstrate cost per 1M tokens and potential savings with batching/quantization, 4) validate security posture.
11:35 - Evelyn Park: timeline? We want results in 2 weeks for an internal review.
11:50 - Ivy Chen: feasible — week 0 (this week) gather traffic traces and infra access; week 1 run baseline & tuning; week 2 deliver report and review.
12:12 - Sanjay Rao: benchmark specifics — what load tooling do you use? We prefer an open harness.
12:30 - Marco Diaz: we use an extensible harness (open) that drives both synthetic and replay workloads; will provide scripts (k6/gatling-style) and a replay mode to replay your traces. We'll include collectors for TTFT/TPOT, GPU metrics (util, mem), batch sizes, and KV cache hit rates.
13:00 - Laura Kim: how do you handle cold start vs warm cache? We see cold starts during scale-up events.
13:20 - Marco Diaz: we'll run cold start scenarios: empty KV cache and scale-from-zero, and warm cache scenarios. We'll include percentage of cold requests in the test to match your traffic profile.
13:50 - Sanjay Rao: what about model variants and quantization? We may want FP16 vs int8 comparisons for cost/latency.
14:10 - Marco Diaz: we can benchmark model variants. Quantization typically reduces TPOT and memory footprint at small p99 tradeoffs; we will produce a comparison table for model variants with throughput and quality notes.
14:40 - Evelyn Park: curious about measurement windows — p95/p99 are sensitive to test length; what do you suggest?
15:00 - Marco Diaz: use 10-15 minute sustained loads for stable p95 but include multi-hour traces to capture rare tails. For p99 we recommend at least 30 minutes to a few hours depending on tail characteristics. We'll do short stress tests + a longer light replay of production traces.
15:40 - Laura Kim: is TPOT reported as per-token mean or median? For UX we prefer per-token median+percentiles.
15:58 - Marco Diaz: we'll report p50/p95/p99 for per-token and per-request aggregated metrics (TTFT + total response time).
16:20 - Ivy Chen: capture cost metrics: tokens-in/out, GPU-hours, instance hours, and per-1M token cost. We'll show cost delta if batching and quantization applied.
16:45 - Sanjay Rao: ok. For pilot instrumentation, we need JSON schema for events.
17:00 - Marco Diaz: we'll share an event schema and example logs; simple fields: timestamp, request_id, seq_len, batch_size, stage_timings (queue, compute, encode), model_variant, kv_cache_hit.
17:30 - Laura Kim: perfect. Who owns the benchmark harness setup on Redwood side vs Hera side?
17:50 - Ivy Chen: Redwood owns harness and baseline runs; Hera to provide traces and a VPC endpoint or allow Redwood runner in a test account. We'll coordinate access.
18:10 - Sanjay Rao: any recommended SLOs you'd propose out of the box for our baseline?
18:30 - Marco Diaz: preliminary suggested SLOs based on your qps/tokens: TTFT short (<=32 tokens) p95 250ms, p99 600ms. TTFT medium (33-128) p95 350ms, p99 800ms. TPOT p95 25ms/token, p99 80ms/token. For batch jobs, throughput goal: sustain 2000 tokens/sec aggregated per pod with <100ms per-token compute. These are starting points.
19:10 - Sanjay Rao: those look reasonable. We'll pick final numbers after you run baseline.
19:30 - Ivy Chen: any blockers?
19:40 - Evelyn Park: only the security sign-off and a small test subnet for the runner.
20:00 - Ivy Chen: we'll attach security docs and send an infra checklist.
20:20 - Laura Kim: last question: how do you validate quality regressions if quantization is used?
20:40 - Marco Diaz: we'll run an eval set and compute similarity metrics, BLEU-ish for structured outputs and embedding cosine for retrieval use cases. We'll include a quality threshold in the POC pass/fail criteria.
21:05 - Sanjay Rao: ok great. Recap?
21:20 - Ivy Chen: recap: Redwood to send benchmark harness + event schema + security docs + baseline SLO proposal. Hera to send traces, grant access or run agent, and pick final SLO targets post-baseline. Schedule pilot kickoff on 2026-06-24.
21:45 - Laura Kim: thanks all.
22:00 - Meeting end.

Notes: transcript contains minor OCR-like / ASR artifacts, some acronyms slightly off (e.g., TTFT sometimes spoken as T-T-F-T), speaker overlaps occasionally truncated.

Attachments mentioned: benchmark-harness.zip (link sent via email), security-pack-Redwood.pdf (link), baseline-results-template.xlsx (link)
